discussion.text:
000
FXUS63 KIWX 111715
AFDIWX

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Northern Indiana
115 PM EDT Sun Oct 11 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Warm on Monday and Tuesday with highs generally in the 80s.  

- Low chances (10-30%) for a few showers and storms along and
  north of the Michigan stateline Monday night. 

- Additional chances (40-70%) of showers arrives Tuesday night
  through Thursday. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 115 PM EDT Sun Oct 11 2026

Ridging through the column will provide a trend toward mostly clear 
skies and light winds tonight. This may allow for patchy fog/stratus 
development overnight into early Monday, especially over ne IN and 
nw OH where lows will likely dip below xover values. 

Return flow and associated strong WAA on the backside of the exiting 
ridge will set the stage for breezy ssw winds and highs into the 80s 
Monday into Tuesday. A low amplitude, mid level impulse has 
consistently been modeled to track east through the Upper Midwest 
and central Great Lakes Monday night into Tuesday morning. 
Associated theta-e advection and slight graze of mid level ascent 
support retaining low chances (10-30%) for a few showers/storms in 
the far north during this time.  

A west to east oriented frontal zone tied to the aforementioned 
shortwave sags south into the area later Tuesday afternoon into 
Wednesday. An additional surge of deeper moisture and several upper 
level waves ejecting east out of an Intermountain West upper low 
likely activates the front with increasing rain/embedded thunder 
chances. Highest PoPs (60-70%) favor areas south of the US 30 
corridor. Cooler, yet, still above normal temps otherwise into 
Wednesday. 

Ensemble and deterministic model solutions continue to differ on 
whether a stronger storm system develops into the Great Lakes in 
response to potential phasing (or not) of southern and northern 
stream waves Thursday into Friday. This brings inherent uncertainty 
regarding precip chances and the magnitude of winds and CAA behind a 
cold front Friday into Saturday. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS THROUGH 18Z MONDAY/...
Issued at 1220 PM EDT Sun Oct 11 2026

Clouds from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias can be seen on
satellite starting to depart from west to east. KFWA is still 
reporting IFR ceilings, but VFR ceilings are anticipated to 
return tonight as ceilings gradually rise over the next several 
hours. Clouds will be completely out of the area by 00-03Z. Winds
will be light and variable through this evening and overnight. 
With moisture lingering near the surface alongside light winds 
and clear skies overnight, patchy dense fog is expected to 
develop. For now, have kept MVFR visibilities at KFWA but I 
wouldn't be surprised if visibilities drop to IFR by early 
Monday morning depending on how dense the fog is. NBM 
probabilities show 20-30% chances for visibilities less than 2 
miles.

&&

.IWX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
IN...None.
OH...None.
MI...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

DISCUSSION...Steinwedel
AVIATION...Johnson

spc.text:
SPC AC 111629

   Day 1 Convective Outlook  
   NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
   1129 AM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

   Valid 111630Z - 121200Z

   ...THERE IS A SLIGHT RISK OF SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS ACROSS PARTS OF
   NORTH CAROLINA AND VIRGINIA...

   ...SUMMARY...
   A few tornadoes are possible across parts of North Carolina and
   Virginia through the late afternoon.  Additional storms with
   isolated severe gusts will be possible in parts of the Desert
   Southwest and Four Corners region.

   ...NC/VA vicinity...
   Midday water-vapor imagery shows a dry slot/vorticity lobe wrapping
   through the base of the larger-scale remnants/cyclone associated
   with Isaias and progressing eastward across the southern
   Appalachians/Carolinas.  Surface analysis places a triple point over
   northwest NC with a maritime warm frontal zone draped east-northeast
   into the DelMarVa.  Despite considerable cloud cover according to
   visible-satellite imagery, surface temperatures are gradually
   warming into the mid to upper 70s across eastern NC and far
   southeast VA.  This modest heating has led to the development of
   around 1000 J/kg MLCAPE across eastern NC and weaker buoyancy
   farther north near Richmond, VA (a few hundred J/kg).  The forced
   band of broken thunderstorm activity moving east across NC will
   likely be the primary feature for severe weather across this general
   region through the late afternoon.  A few supercells embedded within
   the north-south oriented band will potentially pose a risk for a few
   additional tornadoes and perhaps an isolated risk for strong to
   locally severe gusts (see MCD 2361 for short-term details).  Have
   added a level-1 intensity highlight for the area of greatest
   tornadic supercell potential through mid afternoon.  By late this
   afternoon, it is possible (albeit uncertain) that a narrow corridor
   adequately destabilizes ahead of triple point as it develops
   northeastward into central VA.  If sufficient destabilization occurs
   and sustained/robust storms also develop, a localized tornado/wind
   threat could ensue prior to sunset.

   ...Desert Southwest/Eastern Great Basin...
   Remnants of tropical cyclone Rachel are currently centered in the
   CA/NV/AZ border vicinity, at the base of a broad upper trough
   covering much of the western CONUS.  These remnants are forecast to
   progress northeastward today, moving quickly through the Great Basin
   and ending the period over central/eastern MT.  Persistent
   large-scale forcing for ascent and the aforementioned moisture will
   support scattered thunderstorms.  Strong low to mid-level
   southwesterly flow will result in occasionally intense bowing
   segments capable of strong gusts, particularly in any areas
   that can experience filtered daytime heating.

   ..Smith/Barnes.. 10/11/2026

   CLICK TO GET WUUS01 PTSDY1 PRODUCT

   NOTE: THE NEXT DAY 1 OUTLOOK IS SCHEDULED BY 2000Z

spc.text:
SPC AC 111703

   Day 2 Convective Outlook  
   NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
   1203 PM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

   Valid 121200Z - 131200Z

   ...NO SEVERE THUNDERSTORM AREAS FORECAST...

   ...SUMMARY...
   No severe weather is expected Monday through Monday night.

   ...Upper Midwest/Great Lakes...

   An upper shortwave trough will develop northeast from the central
   High Plains to the Great Lakes on Monday. This will bring a belt of
   mildly enhanced westerly mid/upper flow across the region, with an
   increasing southwesterly low-level jet expected by Monday evening
   from the Mid-MS Valley into MI. At the surface, low pressure will
   shift east across MN/WI/MI, with a trailing cold front surging
   east/southeast across the central Plains and Upper Midwest. A warm
   front will be oriented west to east across northern WI to northern
   Lower MI. Elevated thunderstorms may develop by 00z near and north
   of this boundary on the edge of the increasing low-level jet and
   stronger warm advection ahead of the surface low/cold front. Cooling
   aloft will result in a plume of steep midlevel lapse rates
   supporting modest elevated instability. Small hail may occur with
   stronger updrafts within the modestly sheared environment across
   northern WI/the U.P. of MI and portions of northern Lower MI during
   the evening and overnight hours. Overall severe potential is
   expected to remain limited by modest instability and capping across
   the warm sector, precluding severe probabilities.

   ...Southwest/Great Basin...

   Lingering moisture across the Southwest and Great Basin will support
   scattered showers and thunderstorms within enhanced deep-layer
   southwesterly flow ahead of an approaching upper low and attendant
   trough. Meager destabilization will limit severe potential, though
   some gusty winds are possible given stronger synoptic flow.

   ...Southern High Plains...

   A few thunderstorms will be possible along a surface trough/dryline
   across western TX/eastern NM as low-level moisture returns north and
   west across the southern Plains. Modest vertical shear and weak
   instability should limit severe potential, though some locally gusty
   outflow winds are possible given steepened low-level lapse rates due
   to daytime heating into the upper 80s/low 90s.

   ..Leitman.. 10/11/2026

spc.summary: Widely scattered severe storms appear possible over portions of the central and southern High Plains Tuesday afternoon into night. More isolated severe weather may occur into the mid Mississippi Valley, and in parts of the lower Great Lakes.
spc.text:
SPC AC 110701

   Day 3 Convective Outlook  
   NWS Storm Prediction Center Norman OK
   0201 AM CDT Sun Oct 11 2026

   Valid 131200Z - 141200Z

   ...THERE IS A SLIGHT RISK OF SEVERE THUNDERSTORMS OVER PARTS OF THE
   CENTRAL AND SOUTHERN HIGH PLAINS...

   ...SUMMARY...
   Widely scattered severe storms appear possible over portions of the
   central and southern High Plains Tuesday afternoon into night. More
   isolated severe weather may occur into the mid Mississippi Valley,
   and in parts of the lower Great Lakes.

   ...Synopsis...

   A midlevel low will slowly progress through the Great Basin with a
   downstream belt of enhanced, mid/upper-level flow extending from the
   southern Rockies into the Great Lakes. Within that airstream, a
   short-wave trough will progress from the Great Lakes into the
   Northeast, while a more subtle disturbance advances from the central
   and southern High Plains into the Upper Midwest. At the surface, an
   area of low pressure associated with the former disturbance
   mentioned above is expected to develop from lower MI through the
   northern Mid-Atlantic into New England with a boundary trailing that
   feature from the southern Great Lakes into the central High Plains,
   where it will link with a deepening lee cyclone over southeast CO.


   ...Central and Southern Plains into the Mid-Mississippi Valley...

   While midlevel lapse rates are not forecast to be particularly
   steep, daytime heating combined with boundary-layer dewpoints in the
   mid 60s to lower 70s is expected to contribute to a moderately
   unstable warm sector by afternoon. The specific details regarding
   convective evolution remain uncertain; however, forcing for ascent
   associated with the midlevel disturbance and convergence in the
   vicinity of the synoptic front, dryline, and lee cyclone are likely
   to aid in diurnally enhanced thunderstorm development. Highest
   confidence in that occurrence remains over portions of southwest KS
   into the OK and TX Panhandles, where the low-level mass response to
   the deepening CO low will be the greatest from late afternoon into
   evening. Vertical shear will be sufficiently strong to support
   supercells capable of mainly large hail initially. Tornado potential
   may increase during the evening with any ongoing supercells as the
   low-level jet strengthens. Upscale growth into one or multiple storm
   complexes appears possible, at which point, the threat for damaging
   winds would correspondingly increase.

   An areal expansion in level-2/Slight Risk probabilities may be
   required in later outlooks once finer-scale details become more
   clear.


   ...Lower Great Lakes...

   Showers and thunderstorms may be ongoing Monday morning within a
   zone of low-level warm advection and moisture transport preceding
   the surface low and short-wave trough. Clouds and precipitation may
   linger into afternoon, limiting the destabilization in those areas.
   However, where stronger heating can occur, the presence of
   boundary-layer dewpoints in the 60s will support at least a
   marginally unstable environment by afternoon. Both low-level and
   deep-layer shear will be relatively strong, and on the condition
   that surface-based storms develop and are sustained, the threat for
   locally damaging winds and perhaps a tornado or two would exist.

   ..Mead.. 10/11/2026

consensus.about: NWS next to four computer models (Open-Meteo, CC BY 4.0). blend = the middle value of NWS and the models; adjusted = blend corrected by our own average past error at the La Porte airport once 14+ days are graded (capped at 3 degrees). Rain chances are NWS's. suggested = what the Daily Scoop's forecasts use (tomorrow and the day after).

bias.note: Average of (forecast minus airport reading) over the last 30 graded days; positive means we ran warm. Used to nudge the model blend once 14+ days are graded.
